metadata.title: The Gate Is Closed
metadata.purpose: Provenance Gatekeeper development log, Week 8 — closing the open API: a bcrypt hashing pivot after passlib broke on Python 3.13, an OAuth2 token endpoint, and a stress test that now has to authenticate before it is allowed to attack.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Onkar Bhujbal. The Provenance Gatekeeper can now intercept A.I. hallucinations and run regression tests automatically in a C.I. pipeline. But until this week the A.P.I. was completely open. Anyone with the U.R.L. could bombard our endpoint, poison our logs, and exhaust our vector database. This week we lock the perimeter with OAuth2 and JSON Web Tokens.

output: Anyone with the URL. There is no auth layer.
Poison the logs, drain the vector DB, forge the ledger.
401 UNAUTHORIZED — the response it should have been giving.

beats.honesty_note: No attack or abuse is claimed to have occurred — the script reports none. The beat states the exposure the open endpoint allowed.

beats.narration_text: Everything built in the last seven weeks assumed the caller was us. This week removes that assumption — and the first thing it cost was a library we thought was safe.

props.text:
The API was internal.
Assume nothing about the caller.

beats.authoring_note: fontSize 88 to clear the underfill floor earlier reels tripped. 'internal' -> 'unlocked' is the reel's actual misconception: 'internal' is a deployment detail, not a security control.

beats.narration_text: Security work rarely goes smoothly. We tried the standard Python passlib library to hash passwords and hit a wall immediately. On a modern Python three point thirteen environment, passlib tripped a fatal seventy-two byte truncation bug. So we pulled the deprecated library out entirely and wrote a small wrapper over raw bcrypt instead. Worth knowing why that limit exists: bcrypt itself only ever hashes the first seventy-two bytes. That is the algorithm, not the library.
beats.new_visual_element: The error, and the wrapper that replaced the library

show.event: left panel lands: the passlib import and the fatal error
on 'seventy-two byte truncation bug', the ValueError highlights terracotta IN PLACE
note lands beneath: bcrypt hashes 72 bytes — the limit is the algorithm
right panel reveals the raw-bcrypt wrapper line by line
ink stamp lands: PASSLIB REMOVED — hashing under our own control

props.sparkLine: The library broke. The algorithm did not.
props.leftText: ValueError: password cannot be longer than 72 bytes
props.hotNote: bcrypt only ever hashes the first 72 — that is the algorithm
props.stampSub: truncation is now explicit and ours, not a surprise from a dependency

beats.honesty_note: ADDITION. The script frames the 72-byte limit as a passlib bug. The LIMIT is bcrypt's own — the algorithm hashes at most 72 bytes, and every correct implementation must decide what to do past it. What passlib contributed was failing hard on a modern runtime instead of handling it. The reel says both, because 'our library was buggy' alone would leave the viewer thinking the constraint went away with the dependency. The wrapper shown is illustrative of the pattern, not a copy of the project's file, which was not supplied.

beats.narration_text: With hashing fixed, we secured the verify route. Now a system that wants to reach the Gatekeeper has to hit the token endpoint first with valid credentials. If they match, the server issues a time-limited JSON Web Token — a cryptographic passport granting temporary access to the service.

beats.narration_text: So let's point the stress test at the gate without credentials first, and then let it authenticate properly, and compare what the server does in each case.
beats.new_visual_element: Ask micro-beat — the prompt that runs both attempts

props.command: Fire the adversarial payloads at /verify with no token, then negotiate a Bearer token and fire them again. Show me both responses.

beats.authoring_note: ASK → RESULT pair: BASK is the ask, B04 is the result (ASK→RESULT LAW).

beats.narration_text: To prove the architecture holds, we updated the automated stress test. Fire adversarial payloads blindly and the server drops the connection immediately. The script now has to negotiate a Bearer token before it is permitted to run its normalization checks at all. The gate is closed — and note what that means for the test: it is no longer testing the parser, it is testing the parser plus the lock.
beats.new_visual_element: The unauthenticated attempt, and the authenticated one

show.event: the request log types itself across the left panel
the first row lands — no token, 401, connection dropped
the second row lands — token negotiated, payload accepted for evaluation
the token card drops into the right panel: Bearer granted, 30 min
both halves hold — refused without, admitted with

props.rowNote: illustrative request log — swap in your real stress_test.py output
props.alertMeta: bcrypt verified · signed · expires in 30 min

beats.honesty_note: The two request rows are ILLUSTRATIVE and captioned as such on screen — no real stress_test.py output was supplied. The closing observation (the suite now tests the parser AND the lock) is the reel's addition: once auth is mandatory, a broken token flow fails every adversarial case for the wrong reason, which is worth knowing before the suite goes red.

beats.narration_text: So never leave a service exposed, even internally. Implement stateless authentication so the infrastructure protects itself by default — and make the unauthenticated case a test, not an assumption.

the test note lands last — assert the 401, do not assume it

props.code:
@app.post("/verify")
async def verify(
    claim: Claim,
    user = Depends(require_token),   # the lock
):
    ...

# TASK: implement stateless authentication.

# Then test the NEGATIVE case:
#   assert post("/verify", no_token) == 401
#
# An unenforced dependency looks identical
# to an enforced one until someone checks.

beats.authoring_note: The negative-case test is the reel's addition, and follows the Week 7 reel's logic: a dependency that is wired but not enforced looks exactly like one that is, until a test asserts the refusal.

beats.narration_text: And here is the prompt worth running once the gate is shut. Give a model your route list and ask which endpoints still answer without a token. Health checks, metrics, docs, the OpenAPI schema — the ones nobody thinks of as endpoints are usually the ones still standing open.

props.command: Here is my FastAPI route table. List every endpoint that still responds without a valid token — including /docs, /openapi.json, /health and /metrics — and tell me which of them leak information about the ones that are protected.

beats.narration_text: Internal is a deployment detail, not a security control. Close the gate and test that it is shut. Onkar Bhujbal, for Humanitarians AI.
